Option B: Twentieth century topic

text: Did Reconstruction fail?
Study the Background Information and the sources carefully, and then answer all parts of
Question 1.
Background Information
Many historians have argued that Reconstruction was a failure. Some of them have claimed that
the Freedmen’s Bureau was a waste of money and that the South ended up being governed
by incompetent black Americans, which led to a period of corruption and disorder. Others have
argued that opposition from Southerners ensured that Reconstruction failed. Recently, a more
positive interpretation of Reconstruction has emerged, highlighting achievements such as black
Americans being given the vote and being provided with education and healthcare. It is claimed
that Reconstruction was a success until it was ended by white Southerners.
How far was Reconstruction a success?
Source A
Their predictable conclusion is that the Freedmen’s Bureau is a nuisance, is served by unworthy
agents and its continuance will produce disagreement and oppression. It is on behalf of the
blacks that they most urgently call for the ending of the Bureau. President Johnson and the
Democrats accuse the Bureau of re-enslaving the blacks by contracts which impose low wages.
The very success of the Bureau in restoring labour is thus turned against it as a crime. Today it is
feeding more whites than blacks. With the little military support it is still allowed by the President,
it is doing its best to promote industry, security, good morals and justice among all classes of the
population. It is true that, through errors of judgement, a few corrupt officers have been taken
from the army into places in the Bureau. But based on one-sided evidence and with hostile
motives, the report is intended to weaken respect for the law.
From an American newspaper, August 1866. It is commenting on the findings of
Generals Steedman and Fullerton. They had been sent to the South by President Johnson
to find evidence to discredit the Freedmen’s Bureau.
Source B
It is shown that the Freedmen’s Bureau has outlived its usefulness and is now a source of
trouble. It is shown that across the South the agents of the Bureau have interfered in local affairs
and upset local opinion. It is shown that vast amounts of public money have been wasted,
and large amounts collected by agents have disappeared. It is shown that the Bureau has
made statements criticising the Southern people, knowing that they were false. Perhaps the
most provoking discovery is that the Bureau has operated to the disadvantage of freedmen.
It is strange that these noisy Radicals, overflowing with love for the freedmen, support a
Bureau which reduced the freedmen to slavery. The attempt to hide these facts proves that
the Republican faction which is in charge of the Bureau cares more about itself than it does for
the truth.
A report in The New York Times, August 1866. It is commenting on the
Steedman and Fullerton report.

Source D
I shall try to explain what was achieved by ‘we radicals’ in the six years of my ‘dictatorship’. In the
county, new bridges were completed, the size and security of the jail was enlarged and a new
court-house was built. The county had never before had such facilities. Yazoo City was under the
control of the Republicans. Extensive improvements were made; new side-walks and pavements,
and a new steam fire-engine. A new school system was introduced with the active support of
the Northerners and the freedmen. It was so popular that wealthy planters pleaded for a school
for their own plantations, declaring that they not only wanted it as a way of improving the freed
people, but also because they had seen that the labourers on plantations that had schools were
more contented and worked better.
Albert T Morgan in his memoirs, published in 1884. He was a Republican and was elected as
sheriff of Yazoo County in Mississippi. He had to flee the state in 1876 because of violence
against Reconstruction.
Source E
After the Civil War ended the Confederates returned to their homes broken in health and in
fortune, but strong in their patriotic determination to begin all over again. They would have
succeeded quickly had it not been for the enemies of the South and Republican politicians, who
swooped like vultures upon the patriotic South.
When the radical element in Congress overpowered the President and took the vote away
from almost the entire white population of the South, they gave the vote to the ignorant, black
ex-slaves. The white people of the county suffered from the abuse of the carpetbaggers. Both the
black and the white people suffered as they have not suffered since. Many a black was misled
into trouble by the carpetbaggers. Under God’s guidance, we reconstructed and rebuilt that which
had been lost.
An account of Reconstruction given in the 1930s by a Southerner who was being interviewed by
historical researchers. He was born in Kentucky during the Civil War. His family moved to
Texas soon after the war was over, and he lived there for the rest of his life.
Source F
The Reconstruction Act is already accepted by the South. It is, of course, criticised by certain
noisy rebels but not many, even of these, talk of resisting it. The rebel states are to be
reorganised and are to choose representatives and senators for the Congress. It is certain that
most people, despite past differences, will participate in the elections. The future promises to be
closer to peace and order than there has been in the South for years. Protests and violence are
less widespread than they have been and there is hope that Reconstruction will be marked by no
hideous tragedies.
From an article by Horace Greeley published in the New York Tribune newspaper, March 1867.
Greeley was a Radical Republican at that time.

text: Was there much support for the Treaty of Versailles?
Study the Background Information and the sources carefully, and then answer all parts of
Question 2.
Background Information
When the Germans were told the proposed terms of the Treaty of Versailles in May 1919, they
were furious. There were many reasons why they thought the terms were far too harsh. They had
expected that they would be based on President Wilson’s Fourteen Points, and they resented
being blamed for starting the war. The losses of territory, the reduction of their armed forces and
the reparations made the Treaty even harder to bear. However, opinion about the Treaty in the
Allied countries was mixed.
How much support did the Treaty have?
Source A
The great mystery was the belief in Britain that Germany was worse off. No doubt it should have
been, having lost the war. British sympathy for Germany was hard to explain. In many ways
Germany came out of the war no worse off than Britain, and in some respects better off. The
one respect in which Germany did worse was that inflation ran completely out of control, so
that the Reichsmark was worth virtually nothing by the end of 1923. The Germans blamed their
monetary troubles on the harsh peace terms; oddly, many British contemporaries seem to have
believed them. In reality, the peace terms were not unprecedented in their harshness and the
hyperinflation was mainly due to the irresponsible policies adopted by the Germans. They were
also successful in not paying their debts, including the reparations demanded from them by the
Allies. The reality was that the economic consequences of the Versailles Treaty were far less
severe for Germany than the Germans and many of the British claimed. It cannot be maintained
that the reparations total set in 1921 was an unbearable burden.
From a history book published in 1998.
Source B
It was a harsh peace treaty aimed at crushing Germany rather than trying to preserve peace.
The terms bore little resemblance to Wilson’s Fourteen Points. Germany lost 10 per cent of its
territory and the reparations were far beyond Germany’s capacity to pay and led to inflation
that was out of control. Germany soon fell behind in its payments and the reparations led to its
economy falling into ruins. However, many in France still saw Germany as a potential threat to
the future peace of Europe and felt the Treaty of Versailles was not harsh enough. They were
worried that the Treaty left Germany largely intact; with a population almost double that of France
and with no powerful east European neighbours, Germany was actually more powerful in 1919
than in 1914. The French thought that Germany had not been punished enough and Clemenceau
was voted out in the next election. In Britain, many people thought that Lloyd George was a hero
because of the harsh terms, but some thought the Treaty should be harsher.
From a recent history book.

Source E
The terms are in many respects terrible terms to impose upon a country. Terrible were the actions
which it punishes. Germany not merely provoked, but planned the most devastating war the
earth has ever seen. It deliberately embarked upon it, not to defend itself against aggressors, but
to make itself more powerful at the expense of its neighbours. I cannot think of a worse crime.
The aim of the Treaty is to make Germany restore and repair. And we must take every possible
precaution that is in our power against another such crime happening. We wish to make such an
example as will discourage ambitious peoples from ever attempting to repeat these crimes.
From Lloyd George’s speech to the British Parliament, 3 July 1919.
Source F
The historian, with every justification, will come to the conclusion that we were very stupid
men. We arrived in Paris as fervent followers of President Wilson and determined that a peace
of justice and wisdom should be negotiated. We left, conscious that the Treaties imposed on
our enemies were neither just nor wise. Those who wish to see the gap between intention and
practice should read the notes to the Conference by the German delegation. It is impossible to
read the German criticism without forming the impression that the Peace Conference was guilty
of disguising an imperialistic peace under the cloak of Wilsonism. Seldom has such a desire for
revenge been hidden by such deceit.
From a book by Harold Nicolson, a member of the British delegation at Versailles,
published in 1933.
Source G
As I have travelled across our country, I have seen that men have been creating a false
impression of what the Treaty of peace can mean. It is a very severe settlement, but there is not
anything in it that Germany did not deserve. The punishment is not greater than it can bear. It is
absolutely necessary in order that no other nation may ever plot such a thing against humanity.
But the Treaty is not merely a settlement with Germany; it is a people’s treaty, that accomplishes
their liberation. The power of the Allies has not been used for their own glory but for the liberation
of people. Not a scrap of territory is demanded by the conquerors. The men who sat around
that table in Paris knew that the time had come when the people were going to live under such
governments as they chose to elect.
From a speech in the USA by President Wilson, 25 September 1919.
